THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURER.
Tim members of trade societies and the
workmen of the towns generally, pay too little
attention to the 'condition and treatment of
the men employed in agricultural pursuits.
More general views, or a wiser consideration
of their own interests, would certainly prevent
an apathy like this. The better-paid, better
-
placed, and more intelligent portion of our
working people should make it an essential
portion of their duty to study and understand
the condition and treatment of the rural
worker, inasmuch as his evil plight is a con-
stant source of danger to them by his rough
but injurious competition with the half-skilled
artisans of the towns. It would be a waste of
time to touch the controversy as to the Social
condition of the worker iu our fields. In intellect
he is a child, in position a helot; in condition a
squalid outcast, he knows nothing of the past;
his knowledge of the present is limited to the
fields he works in. And the half-understood
utterances of the rural curate give him the only
gleam that comes to him of the future, and
that relates but very remotely to his destiny
as a man in this world. Church and State,
so full of contradictory and confusing ideas to
others, have no meaning whatever for him.
These terms in thar larger and fuller sense
cannot penetrate the solid darkness by which
his dull intellect is surrounded. The squire is.
his king, the parson his deity, the taproom. his
highest conception, of earthly, bliss. Ho has
not the active intelligence of a Chinaman, the
pastoral independence of the Thibetian, the
dignity of the Zulu, 'the ease and the
abundance of the South Sea savage, or the
unconstrained liberty of the red Indian. To
him belong all the disadvantages, with scarcely
any of the advantages of civilised life.. Ho
is a living reproach to all who have had any-
thing to do with him. He is neither instruc-
ted, nor fed, " clothed, nor lodged," or in any
way treated as a human creature should be in
a country pretending to be civilized. His
empty head and stennacb, his smock frock and
squalid cottage—all that is his—point re-
proaohfully to those who own the broad acres
of, England, or who preach in her churches.
There ought to be no necessity to appeal on
behalf of the peasant to men who by their
woaltlt.might be bountiful, or to men who by
their Profession should be thoughtful and
humalle..: 'As matters stand, however, the
hopelessness of the appeal is the principal
reason why it should not be made. After
centuries of relationship
between the lord of the
soil, and the son of the soil'the whole , out-
come is increased splendour on the one hand
and intensified squalour on the other. If such a
state of things is to be altered for the better we
require deeper and more at!tivo sympathies,
newer and more trustworthy aencies, and
more sineere Workers.

We strain no point hero. We invent
nothing—omit nothing—alter nothing. The
statement is a simple one, and easily
understood. There is nothing about want
of employment in it, or illness, or any
common contingency by which family
expenses are ordinarily increased. We
can listen with admiration to the eloquence of
the House of Commons, and, so far as such a
thing is fairly possible, we can admire, with
Lord HOUGAITON, the House of Lords on those
great nights when it presents such an im-
posing aspect to the world. .We can bow
down to political economists when, in their
own dismal way, they explain the laws by ,
tlich the world's business is regulated. And
we can reverence those teachers of Divine
truth, whose mission is higher and holier
than anything belonging to mere mundane
affairs. But we ask thorn all to club their
brains and unite their efforts for the purpose
of removing this scandal from the land. It is
all very well to convert heathens in far-
off lauds. Nobody can object to so noble a
work. It is a right thing also to promote
science and art as a national work, But
before and above all things, and as a tax
on all efforts, the redemption of the English
Peasaut should be looked to. The owner of

property increasing his income by a judicious
employment of his capital, and by active en•
terprise, is a man to be admired and protected.
But if such improvement be made without a
due consideration for the welfare of the man
who works on the land, and if the wretched
balance-sheet given above be an average of the
peasant's condition, then it is necessary that
a firm protest be made against the continu-
ance of a system that produces such an unhappy
condition of things.
It is to be regretted that the agricultural
labourer's condition was not made a subject
for discussion at the Trades Conference this
week at Nottingham. It must be taken up
before long. It is an anachronism which is as
shocking as it is alarming. It does not
synchronize with the splendours of our great
land-owners, and it will be difficult to alter
and amend it, unless earnest men pronounce
decidedly as to the impossibility of its continu-
ance.

There is a social danger here which requires
that we should go to the very root of the matter.
It is true that an attempt at remedy is almost
as dangerous as the continuance of the evil com-
plained of. But leaving things as they are
will not prevent the catastrophe, though it
may leave us without the remedy. To be
wise in time is an admonition of value, and
our squires and parsons would de well
to attend to it. This week a discussion has
been opened in the papers on the best way
of improving the agricultural labourer's
condition. A Mr. PARNELL suggests to capi-
talists connected with the land—in fact, to
men of capital in any class—as a single
practical experiment, to take ten &ores of land
and kuild a four-roomed cottage, let it to a
steady, industrious labourer, and supply him
with the necessaries of life to the extent of
twenty shillings per week. No doubt it is
meant that the requisite capital for seed and
stook should also be found, though that is not
mentioned. At tho end of the year the pro-
prietor is to sell the produce, and after deduct-
ing 5 per cent., place the remainder to the
credit of the labourer, for the redemption of
the freehold. • This may or may not be prac-
tical; but it is a suggestion worth listening
to. Let any man Vrho has a better thought in
his, head state it. Possibly there are five
hundred ways of working out this problem.
Few or many, however, some one way must
be found of a practical, peaceable, and profit-
able kind; or some way neither of a peaceable
nor practicable kind may be attempted. What-
ever the result, the methods of cure for our
social ills suggested by a humane thoughtful-
ness must always be preferable to those
rushed upon by impatient, reckless, or suffer-
ing people.
The history of England is not barren of
instruction as to the danger of social neglects
and oppressions. JACK CADE and " SWING"
made a want known, though they supplied no
remedy; and the lessons they taught were
certainly not of the cheapest kind. The de-
structive turbulence of a week would cost
' more than the practical experiments of a year.
Such an experiment as that suggested by Mr.
PARNELL may be open to objection, but the
controversy and the plans it may throw up
should not be allowed to evaporate in empty
talk. If the coining bu,T season for the
newspapers, brought by the opening of
Parliament, turns such a quetion as
the condition of our agricultural labourers

amusement may prove itself in a very ugly
way some day. England is rich, her people
are enterprising; they are also humane, and
in a certain way willing enough to meet the de-

to improve the farm labourer become a
fashionable philanthrophy ? Itioh men in our
towns and cities have devoted large sums to
the improvement of the condition of the poor;
why do not the Lords of the soil follow their
example? DIVES in his purple and LAzutus
in his rags cannot be comfortable neighbours.
The House of Peers as depicted by Lord
HouonTox on a "grand night," when, sur-
rounded by all that gives it attractiveness and
splendour, may be a very imposing sight. But
those peers on their estates, working with
kindly hearts, thoughtful heads, and liberal
hands for the improvement of the condition of
the peasantry, would be a muoli more gratify-
ing sight.. It may be as well for their own
sakes if they can contribute to make themselves
useful; as mere ornament people are getting
tired of them.

A letter signed "Henry Burbage, Chairman,"

of the clerks up till that time, and the arrears due
up to the issuing of the classification will be paid.
We may state that the annual advance of pay to
the staff generally, the withholding of which in
November last led in a great measure to the strike
in Edinburgh, has not yet been granted. In this
matter the clerks, as a body, feel that they have
been rather cavalierly treated, and should much
further delay be incurred in settling the matter,
not a little disaffection will, it is feared, again
make itself felt.—Daily Review.

articles.title: DUNDEE.
articles.text:
DUNDEE.

TRH IRON TRADZ.

At a meeting of the employers in the Dundee
iron trade held on Saturday the following anal
resolution was drawn up and submitted for the
eonsideratiod of the men :—" That the employers
are willing to reduce, and hereby at once reduce
their hours of labour to 54 per week without any
corresponding reduction of wages; and that in
the event of the trade in Glasgow reducing the
hours of labour there to less than 64 hours per
week, they would therefore, but not till then,
adopt the Glasgow rule, whatever it may be."
At a subsequent mass meeting of the men it was
unanimously resolved to reject the offer of the
masters, and to hold out for 51 hours per week.
The men, therefore, between 1,600 and 1,700 in
number, are now fully on strike.

MANCHESTER.
THE COTTON 'MADE AND TIM TIFTY-FOIM HOURS

110 V EMEN T.

On Monday a meeting of 75 delegates, :repre-
senting operatives in all branches of the cotton
trade in 55 districts in Lancashire, Yorkshire,
Cheshire, and Derbyshire, was held in the Tem-
perance Hall, liirby•street, Manchester.
Mr. Leigh, of Hyde, was in the chair.

The Secretary of the Oldham Operatives (Mr.
Thomas Ashton) explained that since the last
meeting of delegates the Arbitration Committee at
Oldlitan had held a final meeting, and he bad been
instructed to ask the Masters' Association to meet
them on the arbitration. From one cause or
another, however, the meeting had not taken
place; but the masters themselves had had a
meeting in Manchester, at which a resolution was
passed to the effect that the question was entirely
out of their hands, as they had not been notified
by their arbitrator (Mr. Higgin) that negotiations
were at an end.

Mr. Ashton said he had received a letter from
the arbitrator on the operatives' account, stating
that negoaiations were at an end, and that Sunday's
meeting would throw up the whole affair.

It was then moved :"That the agitation for
shortening the hours to 53 per week be given up
front this date."

The motion was seconded and carried. Th ore
were ten
.dissentients.

The deputation from Preston moved : " That
owin to the rapid extension of the cotton trade
since 1850, during which time an inferior material
has boon largely introduced, notwithstanding with

per cent. additional labour entailed upon the

has a strong conviction that the time has arrived
when, having a duo regard to the health of the

moderate but ccnstant employment, and a great
desire to avoid commercial panics, bankruptcy,
and ruin, the necessity for a legislative enactment
largely curtailing the hours of factory labour
should no longer. be disregarded; and it is also the
thorough conviction of the delegates now present
that 6,1 hours per week, so liberally conceded to
other branches of workmen, should constitute the
maximum number of hours of labour in factories,
and to cease work at twelve o'clock on Saturdays."
The reselution was unanimously adopted.

THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE 0001)S orAnDs.

A meeting of the goods guards of the Lancashire
and Yorkshire Railway was held on Sunday after-
noon, in the Free Trade Hall, for the purpohe, of
considering the decision Arrived ta by the directors

in regard to the demands made some weeks ago for
an increase of pay, and a reduction in the hours
of work. The guards are agitating for an increase
of 2s. 6d. per week in their wages, and a reduction

After considerable discussion a resolution was
proposed and seconded, and passed with acclama-

of things, and the delegates were appointed a
deputation to forward to the directors a fortnight's
notice on behalf of the men who had intimated

Company.
• A meeting of enginemon was afterwards held,

TIIII RAILWAY EMPLOYE,

On Monday forenoon, in accordance with the

Mr. Thorley, traffic manager of the Lancashire and
Yorkshire Railway Company, at the Victoria
Station, for the purpose of tendering tho resigna-

men. The result of an hour and a half's conference
was that Mr. Thorley promised the deputation that
he would recommend to the directors at their next
meeting, to be held on the 17th instant, the follow-
ing scale of advanced pay :-225. per week for
guards for the first year after appointment; 235.
per week for the second year; 255. per week for

proposed that 00 hours should constitute a week's

and a half being allowed for Sunday work. Should
however, Saturday's work extend beyond twelve
o'clock on Saturday night, this is to be included in
the week's work. With this proposition several of
the delegates were dissatisfied, and they expressed
their determination to accept of no compromise.
The majority, however, decided that they would
await the meeting of the directors, and that, pro-
vided they would grant what Mr. Thorley pro-
mised to propose, it should be accepted by the
general body of the company's employes.

articles.title: BOARD OF TRADE RETURNS,
articles.text:
THE BOARD OF TRADE RETURNS,

The Board of Trade returns for December
and for the entire year 1871, which were issued
on Wednesday, show for the first time since
April last, a decrease in the general volume or
our trade. So far as the imports are con-
cerned, we gather from an official note
appended to the tables that the deficiency ex-.
Minted in several oases is only apparent, and,
is caused by the fact that in former years the
account for December included the record of
large quantities of goods which had been im-
ported in previous months, but not rcaistered
until the "Landing Accounts" had been re-
ceived. By the system which was introduced
a year ago, the transactions of each month
are strictly included within the period to
which they refer, and thus the figures for
December, though useless for purposes of com-
parison with the corresponding month in
previous years, give for the first time a reliable
summary of the aott al import business in the
closing mouth of the year. To the exports
the same remark does not apply. For Decem-
ber the returns show a falling-off, the declared
value being £16,965A3, against £17,178,058
in the corresponding month of 1870, and
£15,594,978 in December, 1869. The diminu-
tion is mainly in cotton manufactures, the
business in metals being still on the inoreasa.
The following are the articles which show till
improvement :—Alkali, beer and ale, coal,
copper, cotton yarn, hardware, iron and steel,
machinery, silk manufactures, tin, wool, and
woollen yarn. The decrease is under the
heads of apparel, arms and ammunition, cotton
manufactures (8 per cent.), linen yarn and
manufactures, telegraphic wire, woollen manu-
factures, and unenumerated articles. For the
year 1871 the total declared value of the
British and Irish exports is £219,319,071>
against 1199,586,822 in 1870, and £189,953,957
in 1869—an increase of 10 per cent, as com-
pared with 1870, and of 16 per cent. as com-
pared with the year before. The returns as
to the consumption of duty-paying articles
show an increased demand for cocoa, coffee,
spirits, refined and unrefined sugar, but a
falling-off in fruit, molasses, tea, tobacco, and
wine.

articles.title: TRADZS SOCIETIES CONGRESS IN NOTTINGHAM.
articles.text:
TRADZS SOCIETIES CONGRESS IN
NOTTINGHAM.

On Monday the fourth annual Congress of the
Trades Societies and Trades Councils was opened
at the Mechanics' Hall, Nottingham, for the dis-
cussion of topics appertaining to trades unionists
and working men generally, the reason of the
congress being hell at the present period being
that steps might be taken towards combined
action upon any contemplated legislation by
Parliament or from the congress on subjects
having particular reference to the working classes
without the introduction of party political feeling.
There was a numerous attendance of delegates
from various trade societies, representing an
aggregate constituency of 255,710 members. The
official list of deputies included, amongst others,
Mr. George Potter, Leeds Trades Council,
Glass Bottle Makers of Yorkshire, London
Central Society of House Painters ; Mr.
Thos. Halliday, Amalgamated Society of Miners;
J. D. Prior and Robert Applegarth, Amalgamated
Carpenters and Joiners, Manchester; A. W.
Bailey, Amalgamated Society of Tailors; C.
James, General Union of Joiners and Carpenters,
Nottingham; T. It. Collins, Trades Council
Bury; H. Mellers, railway spring makers, Sheffield;
Robert Knight, Boiler Makers and Iron Ship-
builders' Association, Liverpool; John Whalley,
Power loom Workers, Blackburn; J. Sunday, General
Union of Carpenters and Joiners, Leicester;
Mr. Hoe, E. Smith, and Jas. Skevington, Levers'
Lacemakers' Society, Nottingham; J. Rudge and
W. 11. Packwood, Flint Glass Makers' Society,
Manchester and Stourbridge ; Daniel Guile, Iron-
founders' Society, London; H. Giles, Trades
Council, Birmingham ; J. Mole, Operative Pain-
ters' Society, Birmingham; James Adams, Mat
and Matting Association; W. Letherland,
Ricking, John Pullen, and Skevington, Trades
Counoil, Nottingham; J. Davies, United Kingdom
Coachmakers' Society, Nottingham; T. Dale,
Warp Lawmakers' Society, Nottingham; Thomas
Hyland, Papermakers' Society, Maidstone; C.
Williams, National Association of Plasterers, Bir-
mingham; W. Leigh and T. Ashton, Operative Cot-
ton Spinners' Society, Oldham; J. B. Tattersall,
Trades Council, Oldham; W. Wood and S. C.
Nicholson, Trades Council, Manchester and Sal-
ford; It. Applegarth, Labour and Capital-com-
rnittee, Social Science Association; H. Skater,
Typographical Association, Manchester; J. Bunt-
ing, Shirt and Drawers Framework-knitters'
Society, Nottingham; A. Walton, a London
Branch of Masons' Society; Elisha Brown and
Archer, Rotary Framework-knitters' Society,
Nottingham; T. West, W. llill, J. Jepson, and
J. Varney, Operative Lacemakers' Friendly
Society, Nottingham; T. Bit twhistle, East
Lancashire Amalgamated Weavers' Associa-
tion; U. Solly, Artisans' Club and Institute
Union, London; George Howell, London Com-
mittee ; Alexander M'Donald, National Associa-
tion of Miners; George Kendal, Hand Frame-
work-knitters' Society, Nottingham; John Nutt,
Circular Framework-knitters' and Skein Dyers'
Societies,: Nottingham; IL Broadhurst and S.
Mottershead, Labour ReproaentAtion ; William
Allan, Amalgamated Society of Engineers ;
John Sheraston, Brass Moulders' Society,
Nottingham; W. R. Cromer, Branch of Amal-
gamated Carpenters and Joiners', London;
P. W. Stanton, Operative Builders Labourers'
Society, Nottingham;; G.lShipton and G. °tiger,
Trades Council, London; James King, Cardroorn
Operatives' Association, Blackburn; W. Owen,
Potteries District; George Townley, Dressers',
Dyers', and Finishers' Society, Manchester; T.
Oldham, Power-loom Weavers' Friendly Asso-
ciation, Stockport; Charles Matkin, General Union
of Carpenters and Joiners, London; John Dun-
Till° and Robert Byron, Operative Bricklayers'
Friendly Society, Sheffield; William Graham,
Friendly Society of Operative Masons, Manches-
ter; George Thomas, City of London Ladies'
Shoemakers' Society; J. Castle, Amalgamated
Society of Shoemakers, London; J. A. Churchill,
West-end Cabinet Makers, London; J. R. Smith,
Alliance Cabinet Makers' Association, London ;
Mr. Abbott, Amalgamated Association of Elastic
Web and Trimming Weavers, Leicester; James
Forest, Shirt and Drawers' Framework-knitters'
Society, Arnold; and J. Smith, Alliance Cabinet
Makers, London.

The Congress then proceeded to nominate the
President of the Congress.

On the motion of Mr. Applegarth, seconded by
Mr. Nichols, Mr. Letherland, Chairman of the
Nottingham Trades Council, was elected.
At the outset the late chairman, Mr. George
Potter, was chosen pro tem.
Mr. Potter, in assuming the chair, said:
Fellow-delegates, during the few minutes I shall
Occupy this position, I 4411 try, with the usistsnoo

of the Secretary, to facilitate the business of the
Congress. Just before I ask for the delivery of
the credentials of the present delegates, permit me
so say that I hope that a Congress, meeting together
in the capacity in which the members meet, will
endeavour to avoid dissensions as far as possible,
and concentrate itself upon the work which is to
be done, remembering that not only the Press is
upon us, but that statesmen and representative
men of various kinds will look anxiously to the
deliberations of the Congress. (Loud cheers.)
Let us, if we can, concentrate our thoughts and
attentions upon the questions which are to be
brought forward, and do that which will be best
for the persons whom we represent, sinking our-
selves in the common cause, the elevation and
consolidation of the rights of working men.
(Applause.) Now I am sure that we meet to-day
perhaps more auspiciously than we have ever met
under previous circumstances at the present
Congress. We meet at a very opportune time ;
the Legislature will be open to us. The questions
upon which we have to deliberate are paramount,
in our opinion, for the welfare of the masses of
the people. (Hear, hear.) Do let me beseech
the veterans in trades unionism to look
sympathisingly upon the yomnger advocates, and
let us not have any kind of dissension in our
deliberations that may cause any division
that shall injure and damage the progress of trades
unionism. (Cheers.) Now, we have done much
for the elevation of trades unions. We are on
the verge of getting them into a position which
they ought long to have occupied. Lot me im-
press upon you all to try and sink your indivi-
duality into the common good, so that we may do
at this Congress, that which will resound,
throughout all the trade societies in the country
of work done for the country, of work done
for the cause of combination and trades unions
and the elevation of labour. (Loud Cheers.)

Mr. Williams moved that a committee should
be elected for the examination of the credentials
of the delegates; Mr. Allen (engineers) moved a
resolution to much the same purport; and ulti-
mately, on the motion of Mr. Halliday, seconded
by Mr. Allen, Messrs. Allen (London), Woods
(Manchester), and Williams (Birmingham), were
appointed the scrutineers.
The delegates then announced their names and
handed in their credentials, which the committee
proceeded to examine.
Mr. Mundella, M.P., said he had taken the
liberty of asking the Hon. B. G. Northrop,
Superintendent of the Public Instruction Court,
Massachusetts, U.S. to be present, as that gentle-
man had expressed Ilia desire to attend. He had
taken an active part in connection with the educa-
tion and labour question in the United States of
America, and it was with the view of any infor-
mation ho might give that he (Mr. Mundella) now
ventured to ask that he might be admitted as a
visitor to the Congress.
It was announced from the chair that the
question would be taken into consideration when
the Congress was formally constituted.
After the lapse of half an hour, Mr. Woods, the
secretary, presented the report of the scrutineers,
who found that there were represented at the
Congress eight trades' councils and 43 district
organisations; 70 delegates had been duly accre-
dited, representing constituencies amounting in the
aggregate to 255,710. There were credentials de-
livered in, which seemed in the opinion of the
scrutineers, not to have emanated from any in-
dustrial organisation of labour, and the scrutineers
decided to place them in the hands of the Congress
for their acceptance or otherwise. These wore
from the London Artizans Club and Institute, of
which the Rev. 11. Solly was the accredited dele-
gate the Labour Representation League, and the
Workmen's Peace Society, as well as the Capital
and Labour Committee of the Social Science
Association (Mr. Applogarth being its representa-
tive.)
The Chairman (Mr. Potter) said they would do
well not to make the Trades Congress too restric-
tive, but there must be some limit in the repre-
sentation.

After some discussion the delegates from these
bodies were received.

There was a good deal of subsequent discussion
with respect to the admission of the lion. Mr.
Northrop, of the United States, to the Congress,
the principle involved in the question of the ad-
mission of the delegates from the four non-trade
societies again cropping Up; and ultimately it
was agreed to invite Mr. Northrop to be present
during the proceedings of the Congress as a
visitor.

Mr. Howell then road tho report of the London
Couunitteo.

articles.title: TUE REPORT.
articles.text:
TUE REPORT.

To the members of the Fourth Annual Trades
Union Congress, to be held at Nottingham on
January Bth, 1872.
GENTLUAIHN,—Your Committee in presenting a
report of their proceedings during the past year,
must refer in detail to the steps they have taken
with reference to the Trades Union Bill which was
before the House of Commons during last Session.
The sittings of the last Congress terminated on
Saturday, March 11th, and your Committee met
on the Tuesday following, March 14th, at eleven
o'clock, when the following circular was drawn up,
and agreed to, and 1,000 ordered to be printed
forthwith
"TUS TRADES CONGRESS AND THU TRADES UNION

articles.title: brLL.
articles.text:
brLL.

"At the meeting of the Trades Congress, hold
at the Portland Rooms, Foloy-stroot, on Friday,
March 10th, at which repreaontPAives from the

various trade organisations from all parts of the
country were present, the following resolution was
Adopted:—
_ _

That this Congress, having reconsidered the
Trades Union Bill in connection with the ex-
planations and representations of the Home Secre-
tary, hereby resolve that, whilst they are anxious
to obtain from Parliament any legislation that
may enable them to carry forward their efforts on
behalf of the legitimate interests of their fellow-
workmen, refuse in any way to sanction any Bill that,
in its provisions, pre-supposes criminal intentions
or tendencies on the part of English workmen, as
a class.'

"If consistent with your sense of duty to the
country, we should feel greatly obliged by your
opposing all the criminal provisions of the Trades
Union Bill.
"On behalf of the Congress—
" GEORGE HOWELL, Secretary.
"GEORGE Permit, Chairman,
" ALEXANDER MACDONALD, Committee.
"LLOYD JONES,
"JOSEPH LEICESTER,
"9, Buckingham Street, Strand, W.C.
"March 14th, 1871."
The Secretary was then instructed to got
envelopes addressed to every member of the
House of Commons, and the eircalar sent without
delay. By Thursday morning, March 16th, each
member would have received a copy.
This prompt action on the part of the Committee
had the effect of dividing the bill into two parts,
as was desired by the Congress.
But this immediate act on the part of your
Committee gave dissatisfaction to some members
of the Confvrence of Amalgamated Trades, with
whom we were instructed to confer, as it was
contended that no separate action shod(' have been
taken without first consulting them.
It was, however, explained to them that at that
moment promptitude was everything, and we, being
anxious to avoid delay, took immediate steps to
give effect to the resolution of the Congress. The
Secretary was then instructed to see the officers of
the Conference of Amalgamated Trades, and
arrange for a joint meeting. This being agreed
to, a meeting was arranged for the following
Friday morning, March 17th' and invitations
were issued for a joint meeting, but Mr. Guile was
the only member of the Conference present, as
illness, and other engagements, prevented the
others from attending. But our action was ap-
proved by those absent, as our explanation was
deemed satisfactory
It was then resolved that a joint meeting of the
two Committees should be summoned as early as
possible for the purpose of agreeing to a "protest"
against tho criminal portions of the Bill.

—This meeting was field on Tuesday, March 28th,
and the following protest was agreed to, and issued,
signed by the joint Committees :

"THE TRADES UNION ItILTe---A PROTEST.

"We, the undersigned, for and on behalf of the
trades unionists of the United Kingdom, authorised
and empowered by the Trades Union Congress
recently assembled in London and by the Con-
ference of Amalgamated London,
do hereby
protest against any such legislation as that
attempted by the third clause of the Government
Trades Union Bill, based, as it is, on the assump-
tion that acts contrary to law and order are done
and sanctioned by the trades unions of this
country, feeling confident, as we do, that the
common and statute law is sufficient to punish
every unlawful act committed either by trades
unionists or by any other person. We, therefore,
refuse, in any way, to sanction a Bill that in its
provisions pre-supposes criminal intentions or
tendencies on the part of the working men as a
class.—George Potter, chairman; George Howell,
secretary to the Trades Union Congress Com-
mittee ; William Allan, chairman; Hobert Apple-
garth, secretary to the Conference of Amalgamated
Trades."

This was immediately followed by the issue,
on tho part of the tiovernment, of the two
Bills, called " Tho Trades Union Bill" and
"The Criminal Law Amendment Bill." These
your Committee decided to republish, in the
columns of the BEn-firsa newspaper, so that the
trades unionists of the 'United kingdom should
have the Means at hand of ludging of the two
Bills. This, as you will remember, was dorie on
April Bth, 1871. The joint committees followed
up this action by frequent deputations to the
House of Commons, waiting upon individual
members, and explaining our difficulties, and the
reasons for our opposition to the criminal clauses of
the Bill.

Every effort was made to get the obnoxious
criminal clauses withdrawn, but without effect,
and both the Bills passed the Commons.
When the Bills were in the Lords it was
observed that Lord Cairns had introduced an
amendment leaving out the words "two or more "
and substituting "with one or more persons." This
we saw was an intended blow at all picketing, and
would be absolutely fatal to all peaceable efforts
on the part of unionists to give information to
imported workmen, or those coming from a distance
in case of a strike.

Although your Committee obtained precise in-
formation as to the amendment of Lord Cairns
before it was even printed in the Parliamentary
papers, and acted accordingly, yet the action of
the Lords was so sudden, that this amendment
was passed in the Upper House before we could
adopt measures with a view to its withdrawal.
Knowing the great influence of Lord Cairns,

The Northern Pacific Railroad will extend from Du-
luth, on Lake Superior, the western bead of navigation
on the American lakes, to Puget Sound, on the Pacific
Ocean, a distance of two thousand miles, the coat of four
hundred miles of which has already been provided in the
United States.

The route is singularly free from :engineering difficul-
ties, and has grout advantages from its low grades and
comparative exemption from snow, the highest summit
crossed being 3,800 feet lower than the highest levels on
the Union and Central Pacific route.
_ _

The road is completely across the State of Minnesota to
the Red 'River of the North, a distance of 255 miles. Con.
tracts have been let for the construction of the Dakota
divitdou extending from the Red River to the Missouri
(200 miles), to be finished by the let of July next.
section of 65 miles is being built et the western end,
between the Columbia River and Puget Sound. From the
Duluth terminus there is already direct communication
by rail with St. Paul and Chicago. Those connections
will be multiplied by brunch roads now under construc-
tion, and an extension of one of these, in a north-westerly
direction, will reach the frontier of the British province of
Manitoba.

The Northern Pacific Railroad has been endowed by the
Government of the United States with a grant of lands
estimated at about sixty million acres.
The Bonds of the Company are secured by a first and
only mortgage on the road, its equipment, and earnings,
and by a Land Grant which, on the completion of the
road, will average about 23,000 acres to each mile of
track.

The proceeds of the lands, it is estimated, will far
exceed.the cost of the road and its equipment. The school
lands of Minnesota are sold at an average of 0 dole. 30c.
per acre. The lands of the Union Pacific Railroad, so far
as sold, have averaged 4 dole. 400, per acre; lands of lowa

The Bonds of the Northern Pacific Railroad are issued
on a basis of 2 dole, per acro. For every thousand dollar
bond there will always be reserved 500 acres of land, the
value of which will increase as settlement and sales pro-
ceed. The Bonds, therefore, arc a sato Real Estate Mort-
gage, as well as a first lien on a completed railroad and its
traffic. _

--
The- Bonds are exempt from United States taxation.
They are at all times• receivable at 110 U. S. currency in
payment for the Company's lands at their cash price.
trustees are required to apply the proceeds of all
sales of lands to the purchase and cancellation of the
bonds, and to the payment of interest thereon. The
Land Grant of the road, therefore, is practically a Sink-
ing Fund, the operation of which may bo expected to
cancel and retire the bonded debt before it reaches
maturity.
The influx of population on the line of the road more
than keeps pace with the work of construction. Large
quantities of the Company's lands in Minnesota have
been sold to actual settlers. The excellence of the lands,
the Salubrity of the climate, and the diversity of natural
resources within the territory covered by the grant, are
reasons for expecting -an exceedingly rapid growth of
population and traffic. The freight charges paid by the
mining population of Montana, with the present very

several million dollars yearly; and the expenditures of the

supplies have, in twelve months, exceeded five million

Present indications are that the road will from the out-
set enjoy a large local traffic. It passes through the best
wheat-growing region in the world. It already crosses
the Mississippi and the Red River, and the proposed route
crosses at intervals the Missouri, the Yellowstone,
the Clarke, the Snake, the Columbia, the Cewlitz—all
navigable streams, which will cheapen the cost of con-
struction, and serve as feeders, bringing to the road the
traffic of a vast country, pro-eminently rich in natural
resources,

-71.711-ii Asiatic trade is expected to yield a large traffic. By

SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1872.

THE TRADES CONGRESS AND THE
- "MOLESTATION" ACT.

Tug Trades Congress at Nottingham is the
most hopeful assembly of the kind that we
have yet had. Not so much because it con-
stitutes another repetition of the blows aimed
at the foundations of capitalist monopoly,:as
because it has had the personal presenoei if
not the positive countenance of gentlemen,
whose commercial importance and political
position constitute them the virtual representa-
tives of the wealthiest capitalists and largest
employers in the country. The subject which
eclipsed all others in the deliberations of the
delegates, was that portion of the" Govern-
ment Trades Union Bill which was taken out
of that measure and urged through Parliament
in the ultimate form of the "Criminal Law
Araendment Act." The mere title of the in-
famous statute constitutes a foul offence, an
insufferable insult, to the working men of the
United Kingdom; and, as they all know.too
well, the contents of the Ad are even more
hateful and injurious than its barbarous de-
signation.

We always said that the working men
would never put up with it, and the members
of Parliament who were in Nottingham during
the sittings of the Congress will be able to
assure Mr. GLADSTONE that he made a
great mistake when he allowed Mr.
BRUCE, a colleague, fruitful only in mischief,
to fling this defiance in the face of millions of
men whom he was pretending to conciliate.
The real nature, and therefore the deliberate
design of this obnoxious enactment MS
forcibly illustrated by a delegate from Bol-
ton. It has been put into operation against a
member, of his own lodge. All, it was ex-
plained, that he had done was to ask some
man or men for the arrears due to their
benefit society. There is no chance of any
man who once knew it having forgotten the
clause of the Act which lies in Wait to pounce
upon the daring individual who has the
temerity to accost another at the gates of
an employer. The person in question had the
audacity to perpetrate this huge offence.
Without delay he was carried ,before the
magistrates, most probably employers them-
solves; and, upon evidense of the simple fact
on the testimony of a single witness, he was
held guilty of molestation, -with a view te
coerce and intimidate, and sent to prison for a
month. This is but one of several similar
cases in Bolton only, not to speak Of what has
been done in other places. Will theexistence
of a law liable to such abuse be patiently en-
dured? It is impossible. Government and
Parliament must see that what was done by
the Trades Unions Act to tranquillise the
working classes has been undone, and much
more than that, by the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act, an act whose title and oontents,
had they remained a dead letter on the Statute
book, would have been an insult and a menace
never to be submitted to, but whose enforce-
ment, on every petty and paltry pretence, by
mill-owning magistrates in the furtherance of
individual tyranny and class spite, will, if not
speedily and completely stopped, make matters
far worse than they were before. The history
which Mr. MuNDEILA gave the Congress of the

way in which the Bill came to pass 'in
its present shape was, no doubt, every word
true; and every working man is ready to
acknowledge the earnest efforts of that gentle-
man and some others who co-operat3d with
him. But, had not the measure been in-
curably bad, Lord CAIRNS would have found
no clause into which he could foist the par-
ticular amendment against which even the
Government were ready to vote as too bad ;
and, in fine, we have no hesitation in warning
Honourable and Right Honourable Gentlemen
that pampered Capital must not look for public
applause as ho rides past in his cushioned
chariot, while honest Labour lies languishing
in his prison cell.

EIGHT OF REPRESENTATION AT
THE TRADES CONFERENCE.

THE discussion that took place in the
Trades Conference, at the commencement of
its proceedings, as to the propriety of other
bodies than trade societies being represented
there, was conducted in an excellent spirit, and
disposed of in a very satisfactory manner.

The general impression seemed to be that
the question ought not to be decided on hur-
riedly, or on a too narrow view of its separate
parts. Trades unionism in itself, and in what
may be considered its special business, had
much better be confined to those personally
interested by membership in its affairs. And
any attempt, however well meant, on the part
of outsiders, unless specially solicited,
should be regarded with suspicion. But
then the strongest stickler for exclusiveness
should bear in mind that there is much con-
nected with these bodies, and much, too, of
what is most important for their well-being
with which the public must interfere, and will
interfere, whatever barriers may be set up
either by working men or their employers.
Whenever a strike takes place the general
publio is always appealed to, and public sym-
pathy and help thus evoked are.of great assis-
tance to that side which is successful in
securing them. Then, again, as trades unions
have to be regulated by law, it is a matter of
much consequence to working men that per-
sons not connected should help them in pro-
curing the embodiment of justice in the law,
as the late legislation in Parliament in regard
to the action of trades sooieties proves.

Then, again, it must not be forgotten that
there are many associations which exist for
the purpose of promoting the working man's
interest, by securing for him, in every way, his
true status in all that concerns him as a
citizen; associations which are not political,
and which, if successful in their operations,
must confer certain advantages on the working
classes. We shall not specify these, lest we
should omit some one worthy of commenda-
tion, nor is it necessary, seeing that, at any
moment, when the action of outside associa-
tions threatens to become in the least mis-
chievous, the Congress will always possess
ample power to deal with such a state of
things. At the present moment, the thing
aimed at in the constitution and composition
of the Congress should be breadth of view and
wideness of object. Representatives of all
public bodies fairly and usefully representing
working men's movements ought, we think, to
be admissible. Members of Parliament and
other influential persons should be weloom
and invited to join in the discussions when the
subject had any direct bearing on the actual
condition of labour. With such arrangements
and provisions properly worked the delegates
from Associated Trades could not fail at
the termination of these meetings to return to
the constituents more fully and wisely informed
oven on their own special question, whilst
strangers, or rather friends, would in a like
manner understand more fully the intentions
and aims of trades' societies. It is very true
that parties might be sent to trades conferences
whose presence would be anything but desirable,
or whose intentions might be by no means
friendly. But it will be time enough to deal
with an evil of this kind, when it arises, and
the conference in its totality will always have
the power to do that. This conference is
doing a really great work, and its spirit should
is allowed to expand with a true conception
of its own capabilities and objects.

THE MAYOR OF NOTTINGHAM AND
THE CONFERENCE.

A PLEASING circumstance in connectipn
with the Trades Union Conference at Notting-
ham this week, was the banquet given by the
MAyon on Monday night to that body. Such
an act of hospitality is noticeable because it is
unusual, and it is commendable inasmuch as it
was the first time that so prominent a public
functionary in a great commercial community
gave welcome and hospitable entertainment to
a body of working men, whose business, accord-
ing to the ordinary vulgar prejudice of the
employing class, and the flippant assertions of
commonplace dabblers in political economy, is
to enforce the claims of labour, without scruple,
against those of capital, even when most legiti-
mately carried out.

Truly one of the most necessary things, to
secure even the groundwork of a friendly
understanding between employers and em-
ployed is to break down the old barriers of
class jealousy by which they have been
hitherto separated. And no more hopeful sign
that this needful work will ere long find its
fulfilment, could be furnished than this friendly
act of the Mayor of NOTTINGHAM towards the
Trades Union Delegates. An act of such
generous friendliness could but produce im-
pressions on the minds of the parties present of
the very best kind. Exclusive class feelings
cannot continue to exist if the growth of
mutual good-will such an intercourse is sure to
lead to, is encouraged as it should be. Putting
aside altogether the soundness or unsoundness
of the 0Q0110111i() doctrines held by working
men and their advocates, and disregarding
for a moment the reasonableness or unreason-
ableness of their demands, it is, altogether
better that they should be treated in a spirit of
frank recognition as honest and sincere men per-
forming duties which they believe to be legiti-
mate and reasonable. For some time now the
working men of the kingdom have shown a
strong disposition to settle by arbitration such
differences as arise between themselves and
their employers. They have, as a rule, where
it was possible, put by the arms of force, that
their disputes might be settled peaceably,
after a fair examination into the facts of
each ease. Things are now very strongly
tending in this direction, and, if speeded
by the goodwill of the employing class,
we may soon hope to sea the day when
the industry of England will suffer little
interruption from trades disputes, and when
masters and men, through the growth of friendi-
ness and mutual consideration, will work har-
moniously in all their undertakings, greatly to
the advantage of each other, and very much also
to the advantage of the nation in whose pros-
perity they are alike interested. Looked at
from this point of view, we think the Mayor of
NOTTINGHAM is fairly entitled to the credit of
having performed a praiseworthy and patriotic
act, by holding out, as he did, a hand of
friendship to the working men who this week,
as representatives of the various trades unions
of the Kingdom, visited that town.

articles.title: EARL OF DERBY ON OUR STATE AND PROSPECTS.
articles.text:
THE EARL OF DERBY ON OUR STATE
AND PROSPECTS.

Aim we to understand Lord DERBY as
making a bid for the confidence of the working
classes? He does not seem to have much
hope of the speedy return to power of the
political party from which, by formal avowal,
he does not even now secede. How they can
be in power without being in place we must
leave him to convince them. His best attempt
to demonstrate it, will lack, we opine, the
most persuasive and intelligible argument.
If, indeed, they are in power because they
can help the Government to carry what that
Government ought never to have proposed,
while they can defeat their better intentions,
it would be well for Mr. GLADSTONE to con-
sider before meeting Parliament again, how
it is that his majority upon paper does not
make him independent alike of the enmity
and the assistance of the Opposition. If, how-
ever, as it suits even Lord DERBY to affirm,
the Ministry have pursued a policy which is
revolutionary, and a conduct which is uncon-
stitutional; how is it that the peer who thus
charges them, having, as he pretends, the
, requisite strength, did, not prevent them from

going on in this strange course of popular
democracy and royal prerogative.
Badinage apart, however, we are obliged,
in all good conscience, to allow that there is
something to be said for Lord DERBY'S view
of the case. The Criminal Law Amendment
Act, referred to in another column, affords one
instance. Lord CAIRNS, one of Lord DERBY'S
chief fellow-partisans, was enabled to show
himself mischievously in power, though not
in place. The Education Act supplies another;
and, as to both, the Prime Minister can
escape from the imputation of ignoble sub-
mission, only by undoing what his treacherous
or incapable colleagues have done, or suffered
to be done, and taking care that there shall be
, no chance of the repetition of such perfidy or
such neglect. We leave untouched a great
deal that Lord DERBY says as to both the
past and the future; finishing with the single
observation, that Mr. GLADSTONE has to choose,
and must choose, between proceeding further
in a wrong direction by the malignant aid of
those who want to displace him, and return-
ing to and continuing in the right path,
followed by a majority restored to integrity
and unanimity.
On one subject of interest to our readers,
Lord DERBY made the following observations,
which will not fail to receive such answer as
they merit :—" I am expressing to you one of
the deepest and strongest convictions of my
mind, when I say that, for those social im-
provements which we all desire and which are
in everybody's mouth, we must look to the
community acting. for itself in the first in-
stance, and to Governments and legislators
only in rare and exceptional oases. I knew
that is with many people an unpalatable doc-
trine, but hear with me for a moment while I
state it. What are the characteristic national
achievements of which Englishmen in the
present day are most apt to boast? I think
any one would name—next to our free go-
yernment—our unparalleled commerce, our
unlimited command of capital, the manu-
factures in which we excel, and with which we
supply the whole world, our railway system—
the first-established and the most complete
which any country possesses, and our news-
paper press, to which I will not pay a compli-
ment, because compliments of that kind from
public men are always suspicious, but which
you may judge for yourselves. Well, is not
every one of these things the work, the un-
assisted work of individual enterprise, as
distinguished from State agency? Take again
your trade unions, by which working men
have obtained in so many branches of business
their demand for higher wages and shorter
hours of work. They did not ask help from
Parliament to found those unions, or to carry
them on. They acted more sensibly; they
did the work themselves. Well, cannot you
do the same with the great majority at least of
those wants which are reasonably and properly
being put forward ? Artisans, we are told,
require better houses, and foolish and
fantastic schemes are afloat for some State
machinery which is to empty the towns into
the country. Well, are there no such things as
land companies and building companies? And
is there any reason why in every town artisans
should not be able to build and buy their own
houses, paying for them gradually, as in many
thousand cases they have done already? But,
it is asked, why should not the State under-
take this work? I answer that State agency
is not wanted to give you a house or anything
else at the fair market price, and, if the pro-
posal is to give it for less than a fair price, for
less than it costs, then you are opening a door
which willlet in more than you think for. If
houses are to be supplied on those terms, why
not clothes, why not meat, why not bread?
And so you come to what is simply universal
and undisguised pauperism."

HOW TEM PIPER IS TO BE PAID.

WHAT shall we have to pay for the depre-
dations of the Alabama, the Sumter, the
Nashville, and the Florida? How many mil-
lions for the direct losses caused by these in
destruction actually inflicted, and in the in-
direct losses caused by them to the Government
and people of America in many ways? The
Times regards the whole thing with a shudder,
but draws a kind of consolation from the

statement that the Government at Washing-
ton has not attempted to estimate indirect
losses, and therefore will not seek to enforce
them. "If," says our leading journal, "the
United States Governmeat were to obtain
tho judgment of the arbitrators in favour
of the principle of a full indemnity
for the transfer of their commerce to the
British flag, and the prolongation of the
war, and were then to bring forward a
claim for a hundred millions sterling, there
would be no way to meet it, except by
entering into complicated matters of fact and
inference—as, for instance, how much was;
lost to American shipowners by the sale or tem-
porary transfer of their ship, and how far tho
depredations of the cruisers and the blockade-
running of British adventurers did really
lengthen the war." This, in any view of it,
is not a very cheering prospect ; but sup-
posing such claims as these should not be
urged—confining the payments in compensa-
tion to the actual 1053e3 caused by tho
remissness of the British Government, what
sum, it may be asked, shall we have to pay
for the doings of Mr. Laird and his coinis.
pauions in sending out these vessels, and for
the stupid hesitation of Earl Russell, who,
when he ought to have acted vigorously and
effectively, maundered like a bewildered old
lady about the " onus probandi." —Whatever
the sums adjudged by the arbitrators, there
can scarcely be a doubt they will have to be
paid by the overtaxed people of England,
much of them by working men, who all along
protested loudly and earnestly against the
iniquity of such proceedings. Private speett-
biters became enormously rich, whilst
our statesmen speculated in their policy
in hope of a disruption in a rival and growing
state. • Nothing can well be imagined meaner
or baser than the private and public motives
of these men. They made sure their ends
would be answered and their hopes realized.
The ends of the speculators for money have
been answered. Fortunately the hopes of the
political speculators have been disappointed.
Now, however, that the whole thing has
been brought to an end, and that the only
question is how much shall be paid, those who
have grown rich by their wrong-doing will
slink out of the way, and leave others to find
the money to be given in compensation.
Why should the operatives of Lancashire
have to pay for acts they always denounced,
and tho Messrs. Laird and others not have to
part with anything exceptional out of the
plunder gained by their complicity with the
buccaneering they so actively promoted. It
is to be hoped that whenever this matter
comes up for discussion the working men of
England will speak out—will protest energeti-
cally against being taxed for the profit of these
plundering marauders. We do not recommend
this with the view
.of hampering the Govern-
ment in any settlement that may be agreed on.
There is no fear of the American people mis-
understanding the working men of England
on this point. Their friendship towards the
United States was too warmly manifested
during the struggle to permit of any mistake
as to their intentions now. But our blunder-
ing statesmen, our despicable politicians of the
middle and upper classes, and our commercial
speculators in plunder should be forced to feel
how stupid, how selfish, how immoral, and
how unpatriotic their conduct was during that
groat struggle of law and liberty against
anarchy and slavery. We have to pay now
for the depredations of selfish speculators, and
for the gross and unwarrantable insults and
revilings of such papers as the Times and the
Standard. Their mendacity, their malignity,
and their insulting bravado offended the good
sense of honest Englishmen then as their
cowardly swaggering outrages it now. But
the people and Government. of America will
understand that there is here in the masses a
true respect for all that is noble in their
character as a people, and sound in the insti-
tutions of their great country. And that
however much, or however little, we may b.
called on
,to pay in compensation to such of
oa lessened,
citizenss as suffered by our, privateers
duringthe s
ar, our respect for America will
n
ened, although our disapproval and
theirtew
disrespect for our imbecile statesmen and Car-
thagenian traders and speculators will be
greatly in.orottsed.

THE NEW CUT SUNDAY TRADING.
• Tits nuisance in the New Cut is an old
national difficulty. What Is right and what
is wrong on the Sunday as matter of amuse-
ment or business has for centuries divided
opinion in England. And so long as parish
vestries, or zealots of any kind, have in any
way its settlement in their hands, so , long
shall we have tantalising and unsatisfactory
discussions on this subject. We shall say
nothing about it as a religious question. On
'that ground the argument may be considered
as nearly altogether on one side. Sunday is
net the Sabbath of the Old Testament, and if
it, Was, our mode of action on that day would
take all merit out of its observance. What-
ever may be said on the authority of the Now
Testament, the Fathers, the Catholic Church,
or the early Protestant Reforthers, it is clear
that we Must settle this question for ourselves,
and there is nnhigher ground on which to treat
it than that of public convenience or necessity.
The NOW' Cut is no doubt a most vulgar place,
and, being a mart for articles the poor man
needs for his Sunday comfort, becomes also a
place wherein all sorts of speculators in -shabby
wares. ply their calling for their own profit.
In a great city where abeve three millions of
people crowd upon each other, and whore the
very, poor are packed like herrings in a barrel,
many allowances must be, made for the mere
necessities of every moment. People who have
to live and sleeP in the same , apartment had
better buy their bit of meat and few vegetables
on Sunday morning than. on Saturday evening,
for the same reasons that the rich man, who
is . not short of room, orders his fish,
and certain 'other articles for Sunday use,
home on that day rather than on
Saturday. If all the service in this way
dono. by the penitent', the fishmonger, and
others at the west-end of London, was crowded
into one locality, it would be seen that on this
score the rich are even more guilty than,. the
poor. It is true that many things are exposed
for sale on Sundays in London, which poor
men could very well do. without on that day.
The whole of those artieles sold in Petticoat-
lane might as well be bought on the Monday
or the Tuesday; but then if
,the Ifoundsditch
Jew Sunday markets wore Suppressed, many
poor people would, suffer very, severely, and
as What is done is, no offence to those who
would resort to these places, and as no -per Son
need go there who in hiaconscience disapproves
of such traffic, the offence may be escaped by
each class of persons keeping to it own ground.
Nobody not having business there need go into
the New,Cut on Sunday, and whensueli persons
pass down the intersecting streets if. they turn
their heads for a moment, they will not even see
the offence. If the thing is a nuisance Jet it ,
be abated as much
°as possible, but the cpster-
mengers really have something to say whick
cannot be overlooked with justice. A hit of
fresh fish on the Sunday morning to the man
who eats it, is better than etale fish on what
the Scotch call a "lawful day," and .to the
seller thereof, it may make all the. difference
between utter ruin and the means of living
and carrying on his trade. So many of these
poor people touch so close on pauperism, that
to interfere with them in their efforts to pro-
cure a living, can scarcely be regarded other-
wise than as impolitic and cruel.
But putting aside altogether the religious.
view of the question as well as the question of
convenience, there is much to be said on that
otelass offence. The rich do Many things on
the Sunday which the poor cannot do without
offence, and so long, this is the ,case, people
will revolt against ovet.exaotness in regard
to the poor man, and. will rise up against parish
vestries when they try to settle questions
against the poor whieh have, for centuries, been
mutters of controversy. A good deal of the
argument will be found in the following lines,
-which we recommend to the attention of. the
rigidly righteous

The poor man's shin 'no glaring;
In the face of gheatly watning,
Be is caught in the fact
Of an overt 40t,
Buying greens on a Sunday morning.

The rich man's sins are under
The rose of wealth awl station, '
And escape the sight
Of the children of light,
Who are wise in their generation,

Tho rich man has a kitchen
Wherein to cook his dinner;
The poor who would roast,
To the bakers must post;
And thus becomes a sinner.
The rich man has a cellar,
And a ready butler by him;
The poor man must steer
For his pint of beer,
Where the saint can't choose but spy him.
The rich man's painted windows
hide the concerts of the quality;
The poor can but share
A cracked fiddle in tho air,
Which offends all sound morality.
The rich man is invisible
In the crowd of his gay society;
But the poor man's delight
Is a sore in the sight,
And a stench in the nose of piety.

REGISTRATION OP TRADES' SOCIETIES.

'The Congress then proceeded to consider the
next qttestion on the agenda paper, namely, the
registration of trades'. societies. '
The Chairman Said that Mr. Crompton, who had
read 'a Very valuable paper on the 'first day of
Congress, had something to say on this subjcct,

Mr.. Henry Crompton said the effect of the
Trades Union Act, in his opinion, was that it made
a trades union a law fill association, giving fall

combinations of workmen lawful, and it com-
pletely abolished the old doctrine of restraint of
trade. Every trade union was now in the position

Wain of the 'union. In addition to this, the Jiet
offered to trades unions certain advantages, which

But if they wanted to have those ad-
vantages, the Act requircd that they should
, register under certain conditions. In " his

They gave facilities for the purchase, fielding and
sale of land, and for the appointment of trustees.
The liability of such trustees is limited to the
actual amount of money they had received

embextlemont. In his (Mr. Crompton's) opinion,

Some people thought that a better bill could have
been framed. It might be co, and still he thought

other bill ho would say, a generous act of justice,

honourable and liberal Spirit. (Cheers.)

literated, ,

Mr. Mundella said the Congress could hardly

say that the Acts wore as distinct as any two Acts

him tell them he had just been reading the papers,
and found in the Tinics.a leading article admitting

_Sheffield,
and be was bound to say that the rattening that

bers of the Congress as to what trade societies had

represented as many as 34 trade societies in
Manchester, and not one of them had done so.
It was stated by, several delegates that their
societies had not registered, and it was the general
opinion of the Congress that registration had been
very scantily done.
Air. Halliday said the question really at issue
was whether, by refusing to register under the
Trades Union Act until the other was repealed,
such an action would assist in the repeal of .the
Act. With reference to what Mr. Mundella had
said, they knew perfectly well tlutt the two were

separate Acts. But Mr. Bruce, in answer to the
letter sent by the trades meeting at Bolton, did say
emphatically that they were both to be considered
as one Act. Therefore, the question would come

under the one Act wont] not be simply virtually

He might mention that the miners were deter-

Minister had said that they were one Act. • Who-

They had no relation to each Other.

Mr. Knight then moved that, "Seeing that the
Trades Union Act was separate and apart from
the Criminal Law Amendment Act, this Congress
now assembled considers it unwise to refuse, as a
Congress, to register under the Trades Union Act,
as it gives us priviler,e3 which we have not here-

had registered under the Act.

Mr.-Allen spoke in favour of registration, but

Seeing that the Trades Union Act is separate and

A sharp passage of arms, simply upon a point

Immediately after the Congress resumed, the

Mr. Maedonnell, on rising to open this ques-
tion, wished to bo allowed to occupy a low

Legislation in connection with mines was of

COUPENSATION TO WOBICNIEN'S

Mr. Macdonald, in introducing the question of
the necessity of a now Compensation to Workmen's
Bill, said he had taken an interest in the matter for

—(applause.) There was a bill proposed for mak-

present law, Mr. Halliday ended by saying that a

introduced as soon as was possible.

spoke to similar effect, after which Congress agreed

liable to action for damages according to the provi-
sions of the said recited act.

Ireland.

" Let us for a low minutes loolc at the necessity for
