and labour is all the capital a working man pos-
sesses, it is as needful that he should unite to pro.
tea it as that they should who lay claim to be-
longing to what is called the respectable and
learned professions. For a verification of the truth-
Ninon of this proposition, we have only to open
onr eyes and look around us, and what shall we
see? Why plenty of men who have given
their lives to certain trades, worked hard, and long,
lived frugally and dressed plainly, nay, meanly, and
very often died paupers, simply because they have
been so unfortunate as to learn, in their early years,
a trade in which there was no union, but each
member relying upon his own individuality, irre-
spective either of the help or the well-being of' his
fellow workman. The consequence has been, that
they have been completely at the mercy of the
avaricious, grasping capitalist, or what is perhaps
worse, the victim of the middle-man, who has
realised out of his earnings what ought to have
gone to make the producer ehappy in his toiling
life, and comfortable in his declining days; but
look a little further, and we shall see a huge por-
tion of our fellow men, such as the casual labourer,
the men employed in tilling the soil, and mon who
earn a scanty living by continuous toil on the sea
as fishermen, &c., just realising ac much as enables
them to drag on a miserable existence, and those
evils arising to some extent for the want of union
amongst themselves will give us to see very dis-
tinctly the necessity there is for trades unions.
Just one practical proof out of many which could
be given, and we shall dismiss this portion of our
paper. A. trade society, well known to the writer,
found itself under the necessity of augmenting its
rate of contribution lid. per week, or 6d. per
month. The members in one district of the union
did not see the need of this advance in the pay-
merits, and, as the result, that district withdrew its
allegiance from the society. This was about the
year 18213 or 1827. The wages of that district at
the time was about 275. per wook. They gave
up the society, and divided what cash there
was, and became individually self - reliant.
The consequence was that they were about
three years without any union, or the mere name
of one, and about 1830 or '3l, their wages had
dwindled down to about 225. per week, and thus
rather than pay lid. per week extra to their
society, they chose, by their act, to allow the em-
ployers to take from thorn about Os, per week in
the shape of reduction of wages. About 1831
they reorganised a new society for their own ape- ,
cial district, the issue is that now their wages has ,
risen to about 30s, per week. This is not an iso-
lated case, there are many others which might be
quoted, but we consider it is (Nilo sufficient to show
the necessity there is for trades unions. The next
item in the programme of our paper is the objects
of trades unions' and we may commence this part
of the subject by premising in the outset that one
object is to make the man a better mechanic, the
mechanic a better man, and this, we believe' trades
unions to some extent does do. A man to be a
worthy member of his society should be capable
of doing a fair day's work, and doing it
well, and from this point is, or ought to be, able
to demand a fair day *s wages in remuneration for
his labour, and this very thought that a man must
be recommended as capable of getting his living at
the trade has been a stimulus to young raw, ox

Crting upon them an influence tending to make
them better workmen than they otherwise would
have been. Had such a stimulus been lacking, and
in this mode of reasoning, we come to the conclu-
sion that the union has an influence towards
snaking the man a better mechanic. Again, the
rules of all well-regulated societies are that no mem-
ber shall be allowed out-of-work relief or donation,
who loses his work through neglect, intemperance,
or disorderly conduct; neither is he :allowed
sick benefit when his disease is brought on through
intoxication, or improper conduct ; neither is he
allowed any benefit of any kind if imprisoned for
misdemeanour or felony of any kind. These re-
straints we think must have some effect on a man's
conduct for good, for his own sake, and thus from
this point we reason that the union is conducive in
assisting to make the mechanic a better man.
Another object of the union is to break down that
spirit of selfishness which is often found in man
when living, as it were, in a state cf isolation, and
which very often is the cause of sending the weak-
est to the wall. It creates a feeling of kindness,
and a desire to help the weak; and when the hand
of oppression would be laid upon one who might
not be able to offer resistance on his own behalf, the
very nature of unity steps in and stops the en-
croachments of tyranny by rendering assistance just
at the time it is needed ; and on this very ground we
believe the avaricious, grinding capitalist or middle-
man hates with an intense hatred any thing ap-
proaching union or mutual help amongst working
men. Only leave each man to have to put up with
what they please to do with him, and you may
have as much union as you please. But the unionist
has learned a more excellent way, and feels that in
some things he must make a personal sacrifice for
the general good of his fellows. But one other
object, and we shall go on to their usefulness. The
union is an honest protection to the fair trader;
it says to the trade Arab, "You shall pay as much
for the labour you employ as your neignbour," and
would hinder, if allowed to exercise its full power,
that undue, reckless, and robbing competition
which so many who find their way into the Gazette
unscrupulously practice. For proof of this we
have only to examine the various estimates which,
come under our observation. Just one illus-
tration : a large gaol is about to be erected in
one of our northern counties; estimates are re-
quested for the ironwork ; about a dozen are sent
in, the highest of which is over £20,000, and the
lowest under £10,000; the latter, of course, is
accepted; the firm commence to do the work, and
the first important act they perform is to try to re-
duce the workmen's wages and compel a greater
amount of work to be done; union men leave, non-
union men take their places, who are compelled in
their isolated position to attempt all that is required
by the middle-man whose conscience so troubled
him that he was in the habit of carrying about with
him a brace of pistols for his protection, although '
lie had nothing to fear but himself, he has long gone
to his reward. But, with his slave driving habits
the work could not be done as it ought, Hundreds
of pounds were lost by bad work, and the cense-
quonce was, that before the job was much more
than half finished, the firm were bankrupts. The
firm who tendered the next lowest estimate under-
took to finish the work. They did so, and,
although they had over £2,000 more than the
lowest contract for what they did, yet it had such
a tremenduous effect upon their finances that they
made up their minds to have no more to do with
ironfounding, but 00111111011,30 coal getting. Other
1 cases of a sunilsr character could be quoted, but
this must suffice, unless some of my brother work-
men may allude to them in their papers. We urp,
it is to stop, if possible, such reckless speculation
as this, which forms one object of trades unions.
It is often urged that our unions drive trade from
our country. This assertion is scarcely worth a
reply, except for a purpose, and that is, that we
may say that if anything does drive the trade from
the British shore it will be the reckless driving pro-
pensities of the avaricious grasping employer, who
will neither pay the wages nor allow the time to
perform the work in a manner of which the work-
man need not be ashamed. Piece work, set work,
and work performed by very imperfect boys and
pretenders at half-wages, does more harm to the
trade of this county than anything else in exist-
ence. Hence we argue that one object of our
unions is to retain the trade in the country by
doing it in sueh a manner as we believe only
British workmen can do it; for proof of this we
have only to cast our minds back for a few months
to Newcastle, and the importation of Continental
workmen, who were brought to that town to super-
sede the British working man, and to hinder him,
if possible, from realising one of the greatest
victories gained in the present generation, namely,
the shortening the hours of labour. These are
some of the objects they might be added to, but we
must proceed to the third and last point in our paper,
viz., the usefulness of trades unions. The first im-
portant itentof usefulness to which we would allude is
that of trades unions standing as a barrier against use-
less and frivolous strikes. Hitherto the twaddle that
trades unions is the cause of strikes has been the
stock-in-trade of nearly all the writers of the Man-
cheater school of political economists, and who have
had but little to base their date upon but the theo-
retic imagining of their own brain, while the prac-
tical workers out of the system know by their own
experience that all well regulated unions are pre-
ventative of strikes, in consequence of their having
to be well considered, generally by an executive of
practical thinking men, away from the scene o' ac-
tion before they are entered into. In all well con-
ducted unions no isolated branch of that union can
strike a shop or a town until the case has been in-
vestigated by their executive or general council
nor can the pArties desiring a strike, and being
connected with it, have a vote on the matter. They
have merely to state the grievance or oppression
they are labouring under, and have to leave the
result in the hands of a committee of men, who an
king to bear on the subject, calm, cool, and dis-
passionate reasoning, and standing, as it were, at a
distance, can well weigh up the results of a strike
if allowed, and very often are the means of bring-
ing about reconciliation, either by delegations or con-

cessions which can be honourably made oraccepted ;
and thus we contend, trades unions, well conducted.
. are a barrier to a great extent, of useless strikes,
Another sphere of their usefulness is, that they to
a certain extent, help to maintain a fair equili-
brium in the wages market; they are abh by balty
to fix a minimum price of labour, under which no
member need to accept employment, but they im-
pose no maximum, and thus they say to the mode-
rate workman unite with us, and if you are
able to do a fair day's work, we will do all we can
legitimately to help you to obtain a fair day's wage,
and thus we ignore the common doctrine that all
men's wages depend upou supply and demand, in-
asmuch as when trade is good we accumulate funds i
to enable us when trade s bad to buy up our sur-
plus labour, at a sacrifice to the seller certainly, but
with a better remit than allowing it to become a
drug upon the market, and thus enable the specu-
lator to adopt a course which would ultimately
bring all sellers of labour down to a level with
serfdom. No dealer in produce can be compelled
to throw his article into an overstocked market if
he has capital to keep it back, nor is the labour
seller compelled to put his labour into the market
when it is not wanted if he belongs to a good solid
trades union, with plenty of funds at its disposal.
Thus we see that one of the uses of trades unions
is to help at least to uphold the price of its mem-
bora' labour, as well as to assist in the shortening
of the hours of his toil. Another important sphere
of usefulness is, that the trades union is a safe re-
fuge to the good member in the hour of his need
and necessity ; and to help us to form some idea
or conception of the value of union in this respect,
we shall lay before you a few figures culled from
the reports of some of these unions. In the first
place, I find that in 14 years, ending with
1870, the amalgamated engineers have paid for
unemployed labour alone £434,383; the iron.
founders, for the same time and cause,
£222,046 ss. 41d. ; and the amalgamated car-
penters, for 11 years (the term of their being a
society), £32,968, or a total paid by these
three societies alone in the time named above,
£689,697 3s. 4td. ; or let us take two of these
societies (the engineers and ironfounders), who have
been passing through the most severe depression in
trade ever felt by trades unions, and whet is the
result ? Why, in four years, ending with 1870,
they paid for unemployed labour alone £320,196
6e. 2d. ; and this, we contend, is usefulness of the
right kind. Only consider the misery and suffer-
ing which must have been averted by the paying
of those sums of money—how many men have been
sustained, on the verge of poverty it may have
been, but yet they have to some extent been helped,
and hindered from hawking their labour about, and
offering it as a useless drug, and thereby reducing
its value, an advantage often taken by the employer
in slackness, thus making it imperative that strikes
should take place, as employers seldom advance
wages unless compelled by a power they *mot re-
sist. Again, for sickness, superannuation, death,
and accidents, the three societies above-named have
paid, in the same period, the sum of £624,229. Is
this not usefulness? We contend it is—usefulness
of a character which can only be appreciated by
those who have been the recipients or the donors,
for there can be no doubt upon any rightly-con,
stituted mind that it is more blessed to give than to
receive. Just consider how many a sick man's
sorrow has this money helped to lighten; how
many a child's hunger it has appeased; how many
a traveller has it hindered from becoming a cool
pauper; how much extra poor rates has it saved; how
many a widow's almost broken heart has it given
some gleam of sunshine too when, instead af her
husband's boom being rattled over the itiOaoa as a
pauper whom nobody owns, be has been decently
interred by the men with whom, in life, he was in
unity, and who have followed his remains to their
last resting place. Old men in the decline of life
have, to some extent, been comforted by the'aid of
this money, and the poor man rendered a cripple
for life, or blinded by accident, has been made to
feel that, though darkness surrounded him, yet
there has been a tinge of light given by the society,
which, to him, has appeared in the hour of his need
ar the shadow of a great rock in a weary land,.
There are but a few things which might he said of
trades union, but they are, we think, sufficient to
show that there is a necessity fur union, that the
objects of' the union are noble and grand in helping
to form a man's character, and that their useful-
ness is of such a character that children yet unborn
will live to bless such unions, if the members are
only faithful to themselves and their families but
if ever the day should come when trades unions
shall have ceased, other circumstances continuing
as they are, then—and then, indeed—will the glory
have departed from England, and we shell have
become a nation of serfs and slaves, such as can
only be in nations where there is no unity, end
where the producing classes are mere machines,
and gold the god. In conclusion, allow me to say
that the ironfounders alone have paid during 1871
the sum of about £2,500 for accidents, and a many
of these were caused by imperfect arrangements hi
the work, and want of care, produced through an
extreme desire to drive or hurry on with the work.",
Mr. Prior thought this was a suitable thno to
express a strong condemnation of the conduct of
Mr. Scudamore in discharging a number of officers
of the telegraphic department. Ho hoped the
subject would bo brought before Parliament, and
that something would be done to sezure the right .
of the civil servants of the Crown to combine for
the protection of their own interests.
Mr. Knight, of Liverpool, contended that it was
an act of tyranny to disclurge the telegraph
clerks in the way they were. The Government
had assisted Mr. Scudamore in endeavouring
to thwart a perfectly legitimate strike by calling
to the aid of thiPost-oftlee authorities, military
engineers to do the work of the clerks at Dublin.
Mr. Packwood next read a paper on
" Politics and Trades Unionists." He (lie-
cl Aimed any intention of mixing up trades
)cietie3 with any political party; but contended
that a system should be established by which the
thoughts and feelings of the working classes
eould clearly he tweertained on que4tious connect

with their interests. Such matters should be
discussed in trade societies, and by the Congress,
so that united action might be taken, in order to
carry out the views of the working men. It was
only for trades societies to combine in order to
secure the passing of the bills which were of vital
importance to them.
Mr. Odger said it had frequently been at-
tempted to separate the social from the political
question, but this had entirely failed. It was
their duty to ascertain the views of the unionists
for tho purpose of resisting the encroachments of
the two political parties in the State. He did
not desire to say to what party trades unionists
should belong, but as long as they remained with-
out having a fixed principle, they would be at the
mercy of the two great parties, who cared nothing
about them, except for the purposes of political
bargaining.
Mr. Dermal, of Sheffield, objected to trades
societies being mixed up with politics.
After some discussion the motion was carried.

A debate afterwards took place on the truck
system. Mr. Mundella, M.P., said the Govern-
ment had promised to bring in a bill next year to
abolish the truck system.
The congress then adjourned.

DINNER BY THE MAYOR OF NOTTING-
HAM TO THE DELEGATES.

The delegates attending the Congress were
entertained at dinner on Monday evening, at the
Exchange, by the Mayor, Mr. W. G. Ward.
Among those present were Mr. A. J. Mundella,
M.P., Hon. A. Herbert, M.P., Mr, Seeley, M.P.,
and Mr. S. Morley, M.P.
The Mayor proposed the Queen's, health, and
the health of the Prince or Wales, &c., which was
drunk enthusiastically.
The Mayor proposed "Prosperity to the Work-
ing Claises," coupled with the names of Mr.
Applegarth and Mr. Potter. ,
Mr. Applegarth, in responding, expressed his
pleasure that, whereas ton years ago trade union-
ists could hardly find a place in Nottingham in which
to meet, they were now the guests of the Mayor.
The working classes might also be oongratulated
that public opinion now drew a line which a few
years ago was not drawn between those who did
deeds which disgraced the cause of labour, and
those who had spent their lives in legitimate efforts
to elevate the labouring classes.
Mr. Potter observed that twelve years ago he
was called from the bench to conduct a movement
for obtaining the concession of the nine hours, and
he was laughed to scorn. Now the nine hours
was established all over the land. The Mayor of
Nottingham was the first mayor who had yet
entertained the delegates of trades unions, and he
looked upon such a circumstsnce as the sign of a
new epoch.
Mr. Morley, Mr. Seeley, and the Hon. A.
Herbert, responded to the toast of the House of
Commons.

Mr. Morley said he should he thankful to see
working men present a united front, so as to en-
sure a remedy for any grievance under which they
might suffer. He wished the delegates God-speed
in their endeavours to arrange the question be-
tween capital and labour. Millions were involved
in what they did, and the consequences of mis-
takes might be terrible. Workingmen had not as
yet shared, as they ought to have done, in the
prosperity of the country. He should be thankful
to anyone who could settle the question for him
what he ought to pay to bie workpeople, whose
faithful labour had made his wealth. It was a
great embarrassment to him what to do with his
aged workmen, but his firm determination was to
keep them out of the workhouse. (Cheers.) Let
the delegates continue to discountenance appeals
to forse. Strikes might be a necessity, and had
sometimes been productive of great good, but for
the most part they were sources of unmistakable
mischief; not only on account of the immediate
ruin which they caused, but more, because of the
bitterness which they introduced into a relation-
ship that ought to be one of kindly sympathy and
respect.
: Mr: Seeley urged working men to acquire pro-
perty, and become themselves the capitalists of
England. Until they had realiesd property he
could not feel that they were freemen. If a
million artisans could raise 2s. a week, and invest
tto monoy in trade so as to obtain 10 per cent.
interest, they would in thirty-five years have
accumulated a capital equal to that which was at
present employed in trade and commerce.
The Hon. Auheren Herbert said he saw in the
present triumphs of the working' classes and their
improved position the earnest of further triumphs,
and still greater improvements, He advocated
self-help as opposed to looking to the Government.
When they saw a Government take on itself the
responsibility that ought to rest upon the shoulders
of the people, they saw that the vigour of the
national character was sapped, that Sharper dills-
.
rences 4roso between class and class, and that the
people lost the habit of helping themselves. He
trusted that trades unions were soon to pass out of
their fighting stage and that the days when
capital was employed lairshly and unjustly against
labour were days of the past. He looked upon
trades unions as being about to ally themselves
with co-oporation and industrial partnerships, and
to become, not simply organised bodies for settling
the rate of wages, but great instruments for rais-
ing and bettering in every respect the social life
and condition of the members who belonged to
them. •

Mr. Odger proposed, " Success to Boards of
Arbitration, and future harmony between capital
and labour," soupled with the name of Mr. Mun.
della. He drew a sketch of the evils caused by
strikes, and said he had never yet met a man of
the working classes who liked a strike for its own
sake.

Mr. Mundella responded in a speech in support
of arbitration, Ile hoped that in the coming
session Parliarnent was going to do some really
good work, for there were certain things which
only Parliament could do. He believed that legis-
lation about the infamou truck system would be

sharp and rapid, and would root it out. lie re-
commended the delegates to endeavour to settle
the question of child labour.
The proceedings were very interesting and en-
thusiastic.

articles.title: BREAKFAST.
articles.text:
THE BREAKFAST.

The members of the Trades Congress were enter-
tained on Wednesday morning at a breakfast, to
which invitations had been sent by Messrs.
Morley, Mundella, C. Seeley, jun., and the Hon.
Auberon Herbert. The breakfast was partaken of
atthe Exchange Rooms, Mr. S. Morley, M.P.,in the
chair. After breakfast, the hon. member said be
wished to express the pleasure which ho felt, in
conjunction with his friends who had invited the
delegates, in meeting them. He strongly recom-
mended arbitration as the best means of settl-
ing trade disputes. He hal all his life been
satisfied that the introduction of force—which did
not mean argument—which did not mean the
settlement of disputes on high moral grounds—was
against the interests of both masters and work-
men, and therefore he rejoiced to find that every-
where the principle of arbitration was being recog•
nised. If the masters and workmen wera careful
to be properly represented on the Boards, they
would got such a settlement of disputes as
should be satisfactory to both sides. The work-
men, however, must take into account that
there were two aides to every question. That
was the difficulty. Strong-minded men, who had
arrived at the conclusion that they had taken up a
proper ground, were not easily convinced that they
were wrong. (Hoar, hear.) He had faith in many
of the men who were present, because he believed
that they took sound views of the working classes.
He (Mr. Morley) wished sometimes, however, that
he heard more of the obligations and duties as
well as the rights of the workins classes.
(Cheers.) He was not going to advise in the
slightest degree, except that he had the conviction
that if they were simply seeking to promote the
social welfare of the working classes—an object
most thoroughly desirable—and not also endea-
vouring to get into the minds of such men the
conviction that they should rise up to the respon-
sibility of their better condition, they would be
simply securing, as a result, the increase of the
animal instead of bringing out the higher nature
of the men. (Loud cheers.) The country ex-
pected great things of working men, and to come
up to the expectation it was necessary for the
working men to husband their resources. When
It was remembered that the wages paid annually
amounted to no less than four hundred and eighty
millions, it would be seen that a larger proportion
ought to be husbanded than was done at
present. (Hear, hear.) If the working
men chose' they might have a money power
which would bring with it a moral influence
that would make them perfectly irresistible.
(Applause.)
Mr. Mundella, M.P., hoped that the working
men would not forget the condition of children in
mines and factories, which were of the deepest
import to the community at large.
The Rev. P. Morse, the Vicar of Nottingham,
made an able address, inculcating the necessity of
religious feeling and principles in all their acts,
and the higher their purposes and objects, the
more their education would fit them for their
greater and more exalted position.
Mr. Daniel Guile expressed his belief that the
working classes as a body bad the highest and
holiest aspirations fer their fellow men, and felt
that the relations between master and man would
cease soon to be what it had formerly been, the
relation of slave and slave-master. (Great
Cheers.)
Mr. Macdonald endorsed the opinion of the last
speaker, and the company than adjourned to the
Mechanics' Hall for business.

The letter said to havn been addressed by
the Pope to Mgr. Dupanloup, congratulatins
him on his withdrawal from the Academy, is
declared to be apocryphal, and is believed to
have been written by the editor of the Cloche.

It is stated that Prince Bismarck has in-
formed M. Biron, the French Minister at
Berlin, that tho celebrated despatch of the Ist
December was intended to allay irritation in
Germany and not to embarrass the Govern-
ment of France.

A telegram from Kiel, dated Tuesday, states
that instructions have been received to stop
the getting ready for sea of the ships under
orders for the Atlantic, The naval reserves,
which had been called out, are to be sent home
on furlough.

From the returns of the French elections
now published, it appears that most of the
sucoessful candidates are Radical Republicans.
An old Bonapartist has, however, been elected
in the Pas de Calais, and another in the de-
partment of the Basses Pyrenees. •

Last week the aggregate mortality in London
and twenty other large towns of the United
Kingdom was at the rate of 28 deaths annually
to every thousand persons estimated to be
living. In the metropolis 2,452 births and
2,919 deaths were registered, the former having

pox, 67 from measles, 24 from scarlet fever, 3

certified as typhus, 26 as enteric or typhoid,
and 12 as simple continued fever), and 7 from
diarrhoea. The fatal eases of whooping:cough
were somewhat more numerous than in the
previous week, while those from the other

To the Editor of the BEE-11111:.

Sin,—With great pleasure I saw announced
in the advertising columns of your valuable
paper the intention of Mr. Weston to open a
class for the study of hand-railing, and as I
have known him for some years, and received
instructions from him, I can testify to his
ability as a teacher; and as he has every
facility and convenience for practically illus.
trating and demonstrating problems in the
said art, I have no doubt, if it.was generally
known, many of my fellow workmen would
avail themselves of the opportunity ; but as
working men generally do not peruse the ad-
vertising columns of a newspaper, probably
the insertion of this letter would tend to its
publicity, and I hope aid in the formation of a
numerous class.—l remain, yours, &c.,

A JOINER.

STRIKES.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—The strike in the People's Telegraph
Office, which took place lately, has led me to
consider whether it is morally, however
legally, justifiable for a number of persons to
combine to interrupt the telegraphic pr postal
communications of the country, involving
often cases of life and death.

• A somewhat similar question arises when a
cabman or a boatman takes advantage of the
pressing necessities of a traveller to exact
from him more than the ordinary and settled
rate of remuneration ruling at the moment.
That workmen may and should combine to
obtain the highest rate of wages which the
nature of the work they are engaged on will
admit of, I am the last person to deny, but
that they should do this without notice,
when their employers have undertaken con-
tracts on the faith of their continuing to work
at the existing rate of wages, seems somewhat
unfair. The only complete remedy for this
clashing of interests between employers and
employed is that they should become joint
contractors for the work to be done. But, until
this desirable state of things can be arrived
at, workmen combining to raise their wages
should be bound to give timely notice of their
intention. In the interval thus secured, both
the parties concerned would consider the ques-
tion and probably 'come to terms; if other-
wise, at the expiration of the notice the em-
ployers would have to find other workers and
the men fresh employment. This right to
receive notice would of course be reciprocal,
and employers about to close or limit their
operations would be bound to give notice to
their workmen.

Consideration for others is the duty of all
men in every station of life.—Your obediont

servant,
Jan. 6.

Oat' OWN.

articles.title: LABOUR AND CAPITAL. To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
articles.text:
LABOUR AND CAPITAL.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

On the fifth of October last there appeared
in the Telegraph an article which no doubt
caused amazement to many; so rarely does a
daily paper place before its readers principles
of so exceedingly high moral worth as those
disclosed in its dissertation on "wrong is no
man's right," and "right is no man's wrong."
Such an article ennobles the press, and, as
papers publish only what is likely to meet
with a response, indicates a prevalence of
magnanimous and chivalrous feeling among
its readers—a hopeful sign to those desirous
of seeing order in society eliminated out of
the present chaos. The poor Times, sur-
rounded by its dynasties and the fogs of a most
iniquitous monetary aid banking system, lags
far behind the recognition of such feeling and
the principles applicable to its development.
The writer of the article, though otherwise
quite correct in all he advances, evinces some
confusion of thought in saying "the real force
of justice is pure equality of benefits, &o."
Suppose a traveller, in making a point by a
certain time, breaks his vehicle, and, finding
a blacksmith near by, the only one to do it,
tells him that if not repaired immediately he
will lose £l,OOO. In about an hour the smith
makes the repair, and on the principle of pure
equality of benefits, charges .0.00. I don't
think this would accord with the writer's
sense, or with "the real force" of justice. In
exchanges, as we presume the writer means,
justice or equity consists not in "equality of
benefits," but in "equality of burdens." This
will be manifest as we proceed.
We all want continually for our own sup-
port and comfort those things which are pro-
duced by others. Hence we exchange products,
hence comes trade—buying and selling—com-
merce. Trade, therefore, is a necessity of
human society, and consists of the exchange of
labour, or the products of the labour of one
person, for the labour, or. the products of the
labour, of another person.
It 18 clear, if the exehange is not equal, if

one party gives more of hi % labour, either in
the form of labour or product, than he gets of
the other, either in the form of labour or
product, that he is oppressed, and becomes, so
far as this inequality goes, the slave or subject
of the other. He has, just so far' to expend
his labour, not for his own benefit, but for the
benefit of another. So produce, good and
beneficent, results from trade, therefore the
exchanges should he equal. Hence it follows
that the essential element of beneficent com-
merce is equity, or that which is just between
man and man.

Simple equity is this that so much of •our
labour as I take to my this,
so much of my
labour ought I to give you to be applied to
your benefit; and consequently if .1 take a
product of your labour instead of the labour
itself, and pay you in a product of my labour,
the commodity which I give you ought to be
one in which there is just as much labour as
there is in the product which I receive.
The same idea may be differently presented
thus :—lt is equity that every individual
shouldsustainjust as much of the common bur-
den of life'as has to be sustained by anybody on
his account. Such wouthi be the result if each
produced for himself all that ho consumed,
and the fact that it is found convenient to ex-
change labour and the products of labourdocs
not vary the definition of equity in the least.
These propositions are merely, however, a
statement of the principle of equity. They
leave the question of-the method of Making
an application of the principle still open.
They do not furnish the means of arriving at
the measure of equity.
The amount of burden involved in rendering
a given amount of labour, or given commodity,
is technically denominated the cost of that
labour or commodity; and the labour or com-
modity which is received in return for that
i which s rendered, is denominated the price of
it. Hence, inasmuch as it is' simple equity
that these two should be the equivalent of
each other, the scientific/Urn/um is that cost
is the litnit"(a scientific measure) of price.
The counter principle upon which ell owner-
ships is-now maintained, and all commerce
transacted in the world, is that "value-iellie
limit of price," or, as the principle is generally
stated, "a thing is Worth What it will bring."
Between these two principles, so Similar that
the statement would hardly attract a moment's
attention, lies the asential difference between
the whole system of civilized cannibalism, by
which the masses of human beings are ground
to powder for the accumulation of the wealth
of the few, or the one hand, • and on the
other, the reign of equity, the just remunera-
tion of labour, and the independence and
salvation of mankind.

There is nothing apparently
.more innoeent,
harmless and equitable in the world, than the
statement that " a thing should bring What it
is worth ;" and: yet statement covers m most
subtle fallacy, one more fruitfulof evil than any
other which the human Intellect has been
beclouded by. To expose that error, especial
attention is requested to the technical
distinction between value and cost.

"What a thing is worth, is another eipns-
sion for the value of a commodity or labour.
The Value of a commodity or labour is the
degree of benefit, which it confers upon the
person who receives it, or to whine , use it is
applied. , The cost of it is, on the other hand,
as already explained, the degree of burden
which the production of the commodity et the
performance of the labour imposed upon the
person who produced or performed it. They
are therefore by means the same. No two
things can, possibly be more distinct. The
burden or cost may be very great and the benefit
or value very little, or conversely, In the ease
of an exchange or transfer of an article from
one person to another, the cost srelates to the
patty who makes the,transfer, the hurdeirof the
production: falling on him, and the value to
the party to-whom tho transfer is made, the
article going to his benefit. It is the same if
the object is labour directly. It follows, there-
fore, that to say,, that "a thing should bring
what it is worth., which is the same as to say
that its price should be measueed by its value
is quite the opposite of affirming that it should
bring as
,much as •it cost the producer
to produee it. Hence both rifles cannot
be true, for they conflict with and !destroy
each other; but we have already seen,
that it is actually equitable that cost be
adopted as the universal limit of price! in
other words, that as much burden should he
assumed by each party and to exchan,ge as
is imposed upon the opposite party. Conse-
quently the accepted axiom of trade that
" a •thing should' bring what it is worth,"
proves, when tested by simply:balancing the
scales of equity, to be not only erroneous, but
the very antipodes of the true principle.
W. ARNOLD.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

A Paris correspondent telegraphs that it is
believed in some quarters that the Government
will not press their bill for the imposition of
taxes on raw material. The deficiency in the
budget will be made up by an augmentation of
the existing taxes.

A violent scene was provoked in the French
Assembly on Saturday by the reading of
petitions in which a monarchy was demanded.
The "Left" were irritated by the application
of the term " provisiopal " to the existing
reyinze ; whilst the Right cheered the sugges-
tion that a monarchy should be established.
Tho deputies exchanged a good many hard
words, but nothing worse came of the
encounter. It is reported that M. Cremer,
one of Gambetta's generals, has been arrested,
and will be prosecuted for ordering the execu-
tion of a grocer at Dijon on the charge of
treason. Cromer was in command in the east
for some time.

The disputed question as to the censorship
of the pantomimes. seems to be settled at last.
The Observer has "the best" reason for
believing that the Lord Chamberlain "neither
authorised nor directed" any interference with
the Christmas pieces "in respect of. political
allusions," beyond those general restrictions
with* for many years it has been deemed right
to prescribe "in the interest of public propriety
and decorum." On the other hand, the Era
prints a copy of .a letter from Mr. Donne, ex-
aminer of stage Plays, to the manager of a
London theatre, in which ho expressly states
that " political allusions are not permitted,"
and that "all references to Lowe and the
matches have been struck out of the panto-
mimes for 1871." In the face of this letter,
we must assume either that the Daily l'ele-
graph and the Qbaorver were misled, or that
Mr. Donne has acted without consultation with
the Lord Chamberlain, The words "political
allusions are not permitted" have an unae-
onstOmed Bound to English ears ; . and their
author must be taught that he has ',mistaken
the temper of tho peopleiwith whom be has to
deal.

• Mr. Bruce has yielded to the pressure put
upon him, and has reprieved Arthur Frederick
Brown, a youth who had been sentenced to
death for the murder of a fellow-workman at
Coventry. The evidence adduced at the trial
proved to demonstration that the crime was
premeditated; and the learned Judge who
passed sentence upon the convict, spoke of the
act of " desperate revenge" which be had
committed, and sought to exclude all hope of
mercy from his mind. Mr. Bruce has probably
been influenced by the extreme youth of the
convict.

Colonel Towline has at last gained some-
thing tangible by his correspondence With Mr.
Lowe. The member for Grimsby sent to the
Master of the Mint two worn-out sixpences,
which had been re ru,,a by omnibus conductors,
and he submitted theta as proofs of the deterio-
ration of tho coinage. Mr. Lowe's secretary
politely, forwarded to Colonel Tomlin° two
brand new eixpenees, wbich had been pro.
cured at the Bank of England, that being the
place, as ho remarks," where worn 'Silver is
received and exchanged for now." The ciniet
irony of this retort is unsurpassable.

Mr. Jacob Bright addressed the members of
the Crawshawbooth Mechanics' Institution on
Friday. night. The hon. gentleman spoke of
the necessity of such institutions and Their
value in informing the minds of hie working
people and training them to form accurate
judgments upon matters affecting their social
and political condition. The tendency of the
time was towards shortening the hours
of labour, if men were only • mode-
rately wise, and would keep the world at peace,
the hours of labour would be still further
shortened; and it was therefore necessary that
the working population should be trained to
Make the best use of the leisure time which
they .would obtain. Mr, Bright very oppor-
tunely pointed out that the men and women
who were educated in mechanics' institutions
ought, when they became parents, to take an
active part in the instruction of their children,
and thereby relieve the school teachers from a
portion of the burden that is new cast upon
them, lie recommended his hearers to en-
courage amongst themselves a love for the
highest kind of poetry. In conclusion, he ex-
tolled ".tea parties," at the expanse of "public
banquets," and contrasted the order and quiet
of a tea-party—bruken now and then by the
ehrick of a baby—with the hubbub which
Comes from all quarters of the TOM at a
banquet after the wino has circulated twice or
thrice.

We have news from the Cape of Good Hope
to the sth of December. The formal annexa-
tion of the diamond. fields to the &With
d
territory had been proolairne amidst "great
rejoicings." The productiveness of the
diamond " diggings " wits inoreahing; and a
regular stream n of emigration had set in from
Citpetown to the fields.

Two declarations upon the question of
Home Rule appeared on Tuesday. Dr.
Aforiarty, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Kerry,
states that he is opposed to the movement,
and recommends the electors of that county to
support Mr. Dease. The O'Donoghue ex-
presses his eonviction that there is no longer
any ground for the agitation.

The managers of a" workings men's club,"
at Peckham have been lined by Mr. Ellison
under, a prosecution instituted by the Excise
authorities. • It Was shown that. the olub was
carried on in a building to which the magis-
trates had refused a licence; and the Eloise
contended that the owner of the place was
the "club," the terms of membership being
so arranged that it was difficult to determine
wherein lay the difference between a "member"
and any person who chose to walk into the
building at any time and call for liquor. Mr.
Ellison Imposed a small penalty. '

The Duke of Cleveland. will preside over the
University Revenues Commission.

There is ,a report that the election of Mr.
Brand to the Speakership will. be . opposed.
The John. Bull mentions that a meeting has
been held this week to consider the propriety
of nominating Mr. Bouverie for the speaker-
ship.

Her Majesty and several members of the
Royal Family on Tuesday went to Osborne.
The Princess Louis of Hesse and her children
were to have left Windsor for the Continent
the following
,morning, but, owing to slight
indisposition on the part of her Royal
Highness, their departure was delayed for a
day.

Colonel Wilson Patten, M.P., in speaking
at 4 public dinner at Warrington, has ex-
pressed his belief that the autumn manoeuvres
in the present year will take place in the
north of England.

The members of the Royal Commission of
Inquiry into University Revenitea were

announced that; a baronetcy has been conferred
upon Mr._3lWonnell, late Resident Cern-
nussionor of National Education in. Ireland;

Macduff is the new Lord-Lieutenant of ,Elgin-
shire ; and that Mr. J. It. Quain, Q. 0., has
been appointed to a judgeship in the Court of
queen's Ilenolf.

The Lora Mayor, in presiding ovor the
annual meeting of the British Orphan Asylum,
ort Tuesday, spoke of the good work whit&
had been done through the agency of the
charity, and regretted that there should be so
much vacant room in the institution for Want
of means.

M. Victor Hugo has issued an address in
which, referring to his rejection for Paris, 'he
says that apparent defeats lead to definite
triumphs. The city which Germany could not
conquer will not be vanquished by reaction.
At certain periods society is thnid, and asks
assistance from the pitiless ; any one who
favours clemency is regarded as a public
enemy. These crises, however, do not last
long ; the spurious order produced by the
sword soon gives way to the genuine order
produced by liberty. Paris wishes for
pacifi-
cation an concord. To obtain these there
must be an amnesty. M. Hugo maintains
that, though universal suffrago may have its
eclipses, it is the only mode of government,
and is much superior to force as a power.
" Henceforth, everything by the vote," he
adds, " and nothing by the musket," Paris,
he says in conclusion, which personifies the
Republic, cannot long be displaced by Ver-
sailles, which represents Royalty.

Sir Dominic Corrigan, 181. P., in aletter to
the Secretary of the Irish Permissive Bill
Association, says, " Evory day which passes
accumulates before me the evils which intem-
perance is working on our people, and makes
me feel day by day the increasing necessity of
the adoption of seine measures which, if they
cannot altogether eradicate the evils, will
diminish them. astauch ag our power can do.
With those feelings strongly implanted in my
mind it is scarcely, necessary for me to say
that my untiring efforts will be devoted to the
removal of intemperance from our people,"

' A book almanaolt of thirty-two pages is sent
forth by the City Hat Company, of 100 and
110, Shoe-lane. It is not to the batter, but to
another useful trade, that we look generally
for the improvement of the " understanding ;"
but in this instance, Messrs. Walker. and
Fortesoue, the managers, challenge comparison,
not only in what to put on on the head, but
what to put into it also. They have adopted
a motto which none will cavil at. Done into
English it is, "Lot those wear the palm who
have won the victory." Not only does the little
book contain many useful domestic and
historical facts and hints, but also some good
engravings,

It is announced that Mr. W. If. Gregory
will take his departure for Ceylon on the 21st
inst. His appointment to the governorship
of that island will be gazetted in a few days.
The contest for the vacant seat for Galway
county has been raging for some time. Captain
Trench, the anti-Nationalist candidate, issued
his address on Saturday. no supports a
measure which would enable Irishmen to
settle the details of their gas and water and
railway bills athonae ; but he opposes the, cry
for home rule, which he regards as really an.
agitation, however spaciously it may be dis-
guised, for the dismembership of the Empire.
The prospects of Mr. Blonnerhassert, the
Nationalist candidate for Kerry, are regarded
as very promising.

Mr. Mandella, M.P., and , Mr. C. Seely,
ALE, were amongst the speakers at the annual
meeting of the Nottingham Chamber of Com-.
merce on Monday. The former hon. gentle-
man, in reference to the Bankruptcy Law,
feared that it would never be made satisfac-
tory to creditors. At Liskeard, Sir John
Trelawny, the Senior member for the eastern
division of Cornwall, addressed a meeting of
his Constituents' dealing principally with the
game laws. A resolution Was passed by a
large majority in favour of the total abolition
of these statutes.

•
A movement has boon started to establish a
hospital in London "for the treatment of
diseases apart from the ordinary administra-
tion of alcoholic liquors."

On Monday the Portsmouth Town Council
discussed the expediency of taking steps to
secure the holding of the Easter Monday
Volunteer Review in the neighbourhood of
that town. In the result the Mayor was
instructed to communicate with the committee
of Volunteer officers in London.

In his eharge to the grand
,jury at the
Central Criminal Court on Monday, the
Deputy Reaorder drew attention to the number
• • •
Of oases for trial involving the loss of human
lifa. In every instance the ,cause cf these

in all probability none of the oirenees would
have been committed had not either the
deceased person, or the prisoner, or both, been

be well if some law were passed which might
have the effect of diminishing this evil. In

Ronson, on an accusation of defrauding Sir

rain with much favour as a victory gained by

The Outward Indian Mail passed through

M. Vautrain, the moderate Republican, has

95,433. The majority is thus about 38-,t)0.0.
There Was vory largo number of abstentio44,
A correspondent says that not the slightest

James Fisk, junior—the well-known " Colonel
James "—has heou mortally wounded by a

Hotel. The assassin was engaged in litiga-

,ap.

to be discontinued. Tuesday's bulletin, which

ably, will be the last issued tilllSaturclay (to-
morrow).

An inquest was commenced on Monday at
Grove Hall Lunatic Asylum, Bow, on the
body of Robert Dicksons, a lunatic, formerly
a soldier, who died in consequence of a blow
inflicted with a spade by another lunatic. It
was adjourned.

At Waterford, -a Clerk in the employ of the
Waterford. and Limerick Railway :Company,.
forged the name of the Company on a cheque
for. a considerable sum of money drawn on the
Provincial Bank of Ireland.. . Ha has ab-
sconded.

On Tuesday, a. young man named Cor-
coran, while under the influence of drink,
stabbed his father near Waterford in a dan or-erous
way.

4 meeting was held in Sheffield on Tuesday
night to protest against the selection of &
Ilona in crowded neighbourhood for a small-
pox hospital.

Small-pox is alarmingly on the increase in
Dublin. All the' hospital accommcdation is
taken up, and a deputation ye4terday waited
upon the Under Secretary for Ireland asking
assistance in providing more. The deputation
was referred to the Lord-Lieutenant.

The inundations in the neighbourhood 'of
Oxford have been much increased by heavy
rain. 'on Sunday night.

Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P. speaking at Rock,
dale on Saturday, referred to the vote which
he and six other "wise men' gave against the
proposal of Government in 1870 to increase
the army expenditure. Mr. !Potter stated that
Mr. John Bright has said that he resigned the
pose he then held in the Government beeause
he could not support the proposition; but that,
having regard to the stability of the Govern-
ment he did not persist in his resolution.

• .
4n execution took place within the walls of
Gloucester Prison on Monday morning, The
condemned man was one Frederick Jones, who
was sentenced to death for the wilful murder
of his sweetheart, a girl named Emily Gard-
ner, at Cheltenham.

A coil of rope, supposed to have belonged
to One of the prisoners charged with tho
isienagh outrage, has been discovered. It was
proposed to tie the driver with this rope and
lower him into a pit,

Nameboards of two vessel, marked Marcel

Some interest was attaehad to a case which
